Diplomacy · Long read

Japan drew a line around a court. The timing was impossible to miss.

A Japanese judge leads the International Criminal Court. Russia sought her extradition, the United States imposed new sanctions, and Tokyo joined a ministerial defense of the institution on October 10.

By Yuji Shimizu · Published October 10, 2026 · 20:30 JST · 6 min read

On Saturday, Japan’s foreign ministry published a joint statement defending the International Criminal Court at a moment when the institution’s pressure had become personal for Japan. The court’s president is Tomoko Akane, a Japanese judge and former prosecutor. Russia had requested her extradition from the Netherlands alongside eight other court officials; the United States had announced sanctions targeting the court.

The statement did not pretend that every participating government agrees with every ICC decision. Its central argument was institutional: the court and its officials must be able to perform judicial functions without threats, coercion or retaliatory measures. That distinction matters because an independent court cannot be independent only when governments approve of its cases.

Akane became an ICC judge in 2018 and was elected president in 2024. The court issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine. Moscow, which does not recognize the ICC’s authority, later pursued court officials through its own legal system.

Japan was not merely defending an abstract organization. It was defending the ability of a Japanese jurist to act internationally without another state turning her judicial work into a criminal case.

Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said on October 9 that measures targeting people connected to the ICC were unjust and unacceptable, and that Japan had protested to Russia. The October 10 ministerial statement widened that response from a bilateral complaint into a collective defense of the court.

The timing also intersected with the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The Norwegian Nobel Committee selected former U.N. human-rights chief Navanethem Pillay for work advancing peace and an international legal order. The award and the ICC dispute are separate events, but they turn on the same question: whether law can restrain power when powerful governments reject the forum judging them.

What the ICC can—and cannot—do

The court in The Hague prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression when legal conditions are met. It is not the International Court of Justice, which hears disputes between states. The ICC has no police force. It depends on member states to arrest and surrender suspects, so political cooperation determines whether a warrant becomes a courtroom appearance.

Japan joined the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty, in 2007 and has been one of the court’s major financial contributors. Supporting the institution is therefore not a new position invented for Akane. What changed is the intensity and visibility of retaliation against judges, prosecutors and staff.

The joint statement’s careful language is important. Defending judicial independence does not require declaring every ruling beyond criticism. Courts gain legitimacy through evidence, procedure, appeal and reasoned judgment. Sanctions, arrest warrants aimed at judges and extradition demands aimed at court staff operate outside that process and can make personnel fear consequences simply for doing their jobs.

What happens next

The Netherlands hosts the court and is central to any extradition request made for officials living or working there. Japan’s protest does not itself cancel a Russian warrant, nor does the joint statement reverse U.S. sanctions. Its purpose is to raise the political cost of pressure and to show court staff that multiple governments will contest retaliation.

For an international audience, the Japanese angle is easy to overlook. Japan is often described through security policy, trade and its alliance with the United States. Here, Tokyo publicly defended a court that has faced pressure from both Russia and Washington. That is less a geopolitical pivot than a statement about rules: allies and adversaries do not receive separate definitions of judicial independence.

The facts to watch are concrete: whether additional governments join the statement, whether sanctions expand or ease, whether Russia issues further requests, and whether ICC member states continue normal cooperation with the court. Grand language about the “international order” becomes meaningful only when those smaller decisions accumulate.
